title: How to pick an enablement initiative that actually sticks
summary: Sales enablement initiatives fail when goals are too vague to observe. Five traits, specific, triggered, ordered, scoped, and dated, fix that before launch.
body_markdown:
Quick takeaways


- Define each initiative with an observable behavior, a clear trigger, a priority order, a specific audience, and start and end dates.
- Establish whether reps bring up the topic before evaluating how well they position it.
- Review recent calls for a baseline, then test the definition with a small group before expanding.


"Get reps to sell better" is a wish rather than an initiative.


Most sales enablement initiatives fail before they start because they are too broad to execute and too vague to measure. When leadership asks whether the rollout worked, no one can give a straight answer, because the goal was never concrete enough to test. The program ran, materials were produced, a kickoff took place, and performance reverted to its prior level.


Measurement is only half the problem. The other half, the one that derails most teams, is choosing the right thing to measure in the first place. A rollout built on a vague intention will produce vague results regardless of how well it is tracked.


## What an initiative is


A sales enablement initiative is a plan to change a specific seller behavior that is observable on real calls, for a defined group of reps, over a set period of time.


That definition rules out most of what gets called an initiative in practice. "Improve discovery skills" is a goal, not a behavior. The gap between wanting a behavior and doing it is wide, and a kickoff meeting does not close it. An initiative closes it by specifying not just the behavior wanted from reps, but when on the call to perform it, who is responsible, and how long the expectation holds.


## The five traits of an initiative that sticks


### Specific


The behavior has to be something a reviewer can see or hear in a call recording. It cannot be an adjective.


- **Weak:** "Reps will handle competitors better."
- **Strong:** "When a competitor is named by the prospect, the rep will state one of the pre-approved differentiators that is relevant to the prospect's stated pain point."


The strong version can be confirmed with a timestamp and a transcript line. The test is simple: if two people could listen to the same call and disagree about whether the rep did it, the behavior is too vague to measure.


### Triggered


Every behavior needs a cue: the moment on the call when it should happen.


The trigger also solves a measurement problem. It allows teams to distinguish a rep who missed the opportunity from a call where the opportunity never arose.


- **Weak:** "Reps should tell more customer stories."
- **Strong:** "When a prospect describes a pain point that matches one of the top three case studies, the rep will tell that story for at least 60 seconds."


### Ordered


A rep tracking talk ratio, question rate, and monologue length at the same time will not improve any of them. Three simultaneous targets dilute all three.


Limit the initiative to one to three behaviors, listed in priority order. Start with presence before quality.


- **Weak:** "Improve all aspects of the discovery call."
- **Strong:** "For discovery calls, track two things in order: first, did the rep ask what drove the evaluation at all; second, did they ask it before presenting the solution." Confirm the behavior is happening before coaching on how well it is done.


### Scoped


A company-wide rollout bets the entire organization on an untested process. A well-scoped initiative names the specific team or segment it covers.


- **Weak:** "All AEs will adopt the new messaging starting Monday."
- **Strong:** "The new messaging will be piloted with the Mid-Market West AE team."


One thing worth getting right at this stage: do not pilot with top performers. They can make almost any process work for reasons that will not generalize to the rest of the team. Pilot with a representative group instead, ideally one that wants to improve.


### Dated


An initiative with no end date becomes a standing mandate, and standing mandates become noise. Reps already have too many standing expectations.


- **Weak:** "This year, our focus is on value selling."
- **Strong:** "The competitive positioning initiative runs July 1 to September 30. Training finishes by July 15. We review where the team stands the first week of October."


## Four traps to avoid


**A goal too vague to observe.** If the behavior cannot be written as a sentence a call reviewer would mark pass or fail, it is not ready. Vague goals are the most common reason sales enablement initiatives produce no measurable outcome. A plan is not a plan until the behavior is observable.


**Always-on monitoring.** Reps already receive feedback from managers, their own performance data, and their pipeline. Adding another layer of continuous, non-specific scoring creates noise rather than signal. Applying one standard to every call type regardless of context erodes trust in the data. Time-bound initiatives with a defined scope produce cleaner signal than permanent monitoring programs.


**A trigger that almost never fires.** If the selected cue occurs on fewer than one in twenty calls, the initiative will lack sufficient data. Before finalizing a trigger, estimate how often it appears in recent calls. A trigger that fires rarely is not useful as a measurement anchor.


**Too many behaviors at once.** Behavior change is cognitively demanding. A rep cannot consciously manage talk ratio, question rate, competitor response, and monologue length in the same conversation. One behavior is the right size for most initiatives. Three is the upper limit.


## Four initiatives worth running


Initiative Observable behavior Trigger Audience Duration


Competitive positioning Asked what prompted the evaluation before discussing competitive differences A buyer mentions an active competitor evaluation One sales team Six weeks


Product push Asked the buyer to quantify the business impact of the problem the product addresses Discovery calls where that problem is identified Pilot group of four to six reps One month


New company pitch Named the buyer problem and explained how the company addresses it Company introductions in first meetings A pilot group of account executives One quarter


Discovery skill Agreed with the buyer on measurable success criteria Discovery calls New hires and reps with an identified gap Three weeks


Scroll the table sideways →


Each row in the table passes all five tests: a specific behavior, a named trigger, a single focus, a defined audience, and a fixed window.


## Start small, and baseline first


Before launching any initiative, even to a pilot group, establish a baseline. Call it Point A before you map a route to Point B. Without a baseline, you are designing a fix for a problem you have not confirmed exists.


Two reasons to baseline every initiative:


1. **It turns a feeling into a number.** A VP's sense that "discovery calls are weak" is not a mandate. Data showing that reps ask a clarifying question on four of ten discovery calls is.
2. **It stops you designing for a gap that does not exist.** If the baseline shows most reps already do the behavior, the initiative will produce no visible change, because there was no gap to close.


Manual call review typically covers a small fraction of a team's conversations, so any spot-check is a sample, not a census. Treat it as directional, and size your sample accordingly before committing to a design.


Try this: define one initiative in 20 minutes


Choose a broad goal from your current roadmap, such as "handle objections better." Rewrite it using this template:


\[Specific behavior\] on \[call type or situation\], for \[defined group of reps\], between \[start date\] and \[end date\].


Run it through the five-question checklist. Then identify the recent calls you would review to establish a baseline. You can complete the planning exercise on paper or in a document, without specialist software.


## The five-question checklist


Before you commit a quarter to a rollout, answer these:


1. **Specific:** Would two people listening to the same call agree on whether the rep did it?
2. **Triggered:** What has to happen on a call for this behavior to apply?
3. **Ordered:** Do I have one to three behaviors, ranked, with the most basic one first?
4. **Scoped:** Which specific reps or teams is this for, and who is out?
5. **Dated:** When does it start, when does it end, and when will I look at the numbers?


Five yeses means you have an initiative. Any no is the part that will make the rollout unmeasurable later.


For Hyperbound customers


Start with a scorecard your team already uses. Select one to three relevant criteria and phrase each as an observable "Did the rep…?" question. Apply the checklist before planning the rollout, particularly the rules for which calls count.


## What to do next


Choosing the right initiative is half the work. The other half is seeing whether it is happening once it is live, and doing something when it is not, which is where most enablement programs lose the thread.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Sales Enablement Initiatives


### What is a sales enablement initiative?


A sales enablement initiative is a time-bound plan to change one specific, observable seller behavior for a defined group of reps. It is not a general goal like "sell better" or a permanent training program. A well-built initiative names the behavior, the trigger moment on the call, the audience, and the start and end dates, so it can be executed and measured.


### What is the difference between a sales enablement goal and an initiative?


A goal describes the desired outcome; an initiative describes the observable behavior change that will be run for a set period to pursue it. "Improve discovery" is a goal. "The Mid-Market AE team will ask what drove the evaluation on every discovery call, for eight weeks" is an initiative. The initiative includes a trigger, scope, and dates that make it testable.


### How many behaviors should one sales enablement initiative focus on?


Focus on one behavior for most initiatives, with three as the absolute upper limit. Reps cannot consciously manage talk ratio, question rate, competitor responses, and monologue length in the same conversation. Prioritize the behavior that matters most first, confirm it is happening, then coach on quality.


### How long should a sales enablement pilot run?


Run a sales enablement pilot for at least 60 days of observed behavior after training before drawing conclusions. A shorter window often captures novelty or launch energy rather than a durable change. Build the 60-day window into the initiative dates from the start, and schedule a formal close-out review after it ends.


### Should you pilot a sales enablement initiative with top performers?


No. Pilot with a respected, improvement-oriented group rather than top performers. Top performers can make almost any process work for reasons that do not generalize to the rest of the team. A representative pilot group provides a cleaner read on whether the initiative will work at scale.


### How do you baseline a sales enablement initiative?


Review recent calls to establish Point A before launching, so teams know whether the performance gap is real. Turn a vague concern like "discovery is weak" into a number, such as how often reps ask what drove the evaluation. If the baseline already meets the bar, there may not be a gap worth designing an initiative around.


### What is an example of a well-defined sales enablement initiative?


A well-defined sales enablement initiative names one observable behavior, its trigger, audience, and dates. For example: “When a prospect names a competitor, the Enterprise AE pilot team will state one pre-approved differentiator relevant to the prospect’s stated pain point, from July 1 to September 30.” This example passes the five tests: it is specific, triggered, ordered, scoped, and dated.


### How do you measure whether a sales enablement initiative worked?


Measure the specific behavior against the baseline over the defined window and compare where the team stands to Point A. Use a sample of real calls and count how often the behavior shows up, rather than relying on attendance or completion metrics.


### What are common mistakes in sales enablement initiatives?


The most common mistakes are vague goals, too many behaviors, always-on monitoring, rare triggers, and no baseline. Each one makes the initiative harder to execute and harder to measure. Fix them by writing the behavior as something a reviewer can see or hear, limiting the focus, scoping the pilot, and setting clear start and end dates.


### What is a simple template for writing a sales enablement initiative?


Use this sentence: "\[Specific behavior\] on \[call type or situation where it applies\], for \[which reps\], between \[start date\] and \[end date\]." For example: "The Enterprise AE team will ask what drove the evaluation before presenting a solution, on discovery calls, between July 1 and September 30." Then check that the behavior is observable, triggered, limited to one to three behaviors, scoped to a specific group, and dated.
